scenes.title: 관절에서 손으로, 손에서 관절로
lines: When Donkey Kong swings his arms wide, his hands catch the eye. The range of a bend changes the expression. A skeleton that's easy to animate in ordinary poses might struggle with that shape. We'll look at two ways to control joints, then explore limitations and ways to extend an exaggerated pose. The hierarchy of bones that moves a character is its skeleton. The skeleton and its controls form a rig. Turn the shoulder and the elbow and hand move with it. Bend the elbow and the hand changes position. Setting joint angles from the body outward to find the endpoint is forward kinematics, or FK. Watch a fighter raise an arm to guard. A change at the shoulder changes the path of the hand we see. Now imagine putting the hand on a specific spot on a desk. You could keep adjusting the joints, or set a hand target and solve for the joints that reach it. The second approach is inverse kinematics, or IK. Rotate the shoulder on one side of our grid and move a hand target on the other. The same idea is useful for feet. Set a foot target on the ground and solve the leg pose to fit the surface. Convenient controls still favor some poses over others.

scenes.title: 팔을 곧게 편 지점 너머의 표현
lines: Suppose an extended arm needs a stronger curve than a straight line. A rig designed for an ordinary human elbow may resist that shape. Cuphead’s mermaid spreads and gathers her arms. If two segments made that outline, where would the elbow go? To bend past straight, inspect the bend direction the control assumes. A straight line between the two bones makes a 180-degree angle. That doesn't impose a universal 180-degree rotation limit on computer joints. Bone rotation, the bend chosen by IK, and skin deformation are separate questions. A fixed target for the hand may still need a separate hint for the elbow. We'll keep that target fixed and move the hint that sets bend direction. If the controls resist the exaggeration, change the limit or bend direction, or author that pose another way. Reaching the target isn't the end of the test. Check the surface for collapsing or folding skin. With Donkey Kong’s large hands, the hand direction can dominate the reading of the arm. Decide what needs to survive in the image. A possible pose and a good-looking pose can differ.

scenes.title: 표현을 넓히는 구조에도 비용이 있다
lines: More bones or joints give you additional points from which to shape a curved arm. Compared with a few rigid segments, extra control points let you shape the middle. More controls alone won't create a great cartoon gesture. Choose where to stretch and which silhouette to preserve. There are also more elements to manage and evaluate. One project may choose a richer rig; another may work creatively within a simpler one. Notice Lili’s sleeve. The hand can stay fixed while the forearm changes shape. More controls can shape that curve. We'll build the same target pose with a simple chain and one with extra controls. Compare what each can show and what it asks the animator to adjust. The number of bones doesn't directly predict the increase in running time. Choose with both expression and performance in mind.

scenes.title: 도구의 기본값보다 표현의 목적을 먼저
lines: It's easy to aim only for poses familiar tools make convenient. Thinking within those limits from the outset can hide a need for stronger expression. Decide on the force and emotion first, then choose a skeleton and controls to suit that result. Use FK and IK without treating a specific rig's limits as limits on every character. The skeleton is a tool for creating motion. What we want to move starts with what we want to express.
